I came here to say this. You are 100% correct. Chicken bones are hollow with thin walls as are all fowl bones. It's an evolution thing that makes the bones lighter for flight purposes. Their bones are very strong but their strength comes in the ability to bend, once cooked they splinter. Other animals bones get their strength from density. When a dog bites a hollow chicken bone it splinters where a bone from any other animal will crush. I have a friend that's a veterinarian and he said he has to remove chicken bone splinters from a dog's throat on a regular basis. All the vets that have ever treated my dogs over the years have told me the same thing. If Orphan Annie starts hacking and gagging continuously get her to a vet ASAP. If you don't get it out the throat will start to swell and it can kill the dog.

Here's what the AKC (American Kennel Club) suggests you should do in case your dog ate chicken bones:

What to Do if Your Dog Eats a Chicken Bone

If you feel you must feed chicken bones to your dog give it the back or breast of the bird. Those are the only bones in a bird that aren't hollow.

Vet tech here, let me clear this up.

Chicken bones are fine for medium to large sized dogs. They don't splinter much, and any splinters are easily chomped up, cooked or uncooked.

Dogs are built to eat small game, this includes rats, mice, possums, etc. Despite you feeding them Beneful kibble shaped like little hams and steaks, they can in fact eat actual animals.

The issue seems to stem from dogs swallowing very small bones whole, which can be trouble. Also, we get a lot of problem from quote-unquote "bones", which are actually dyed rawhide. These actually don't splinter, and wide up going down the dog's throat in a large sheet. Stay away from those. But your medium-sized dog (or any-sized cat) will enjoy your leftover drumstick.
